1.pericope_label: The angels of God meet Jacob at Mahanaim

schools.summary: Gill takes the appearance to have been human and soldierly, which is why they are called a host, and reports Aben Ezra's view that Jacob alone saw them; Calvin has Jacob proceeding as one going to the slaughter, assigns the vision the double use of removing terror and fixing the memory of past deliverance, prefers angels ranged on both sides to the Hebrew interpreters' reading of an enemy camp opposite God's, allows the dual to stand for a plural, and rebukes those who allow each believer only one guardian angel.

Henry marks the relief of being clear of Laban, observes that the comfort came in a calm interval because God would have us provide for trouble in peace, reports the rabbinic account of the angels of Mesopotamia handing Jacob to the angels of Canaan while preferring a guard before and behind against Esau and Laban, and presses the comfort that faith sees what Jacob saw and that a guard of angels settles the question of a guardian angel.

Clarke derives angel from the Greek and Hebrew words for messenger and sending, cites Augustine that it names an office and not a nature and Parkhurst on the angel of Jehovah as God's means of visibility, reads Mahanaim as the angels' camp with Jacob's own, notes the later priestly city there, and argues at length that angels may not be invoked since they are instruments without discretionary power; Wesley leaves the manner of the vision open and repeats Henry's comfort about the guard of angels almost word for word.

Ellicott places the parting from Laban on the frontier where he could find no allies, dates the vision about a week's journey southward, collects and rejects the rationalising conjectures that the messengers were prophets, a caravan or a company sent by Rebekah, and allows Mahanaim to mean either Jacob's camp with the angels' or two camps of angels flanking him, noting the town's later importance in Gad; Keil and Delitzsch move directly from the naming to the embassy sent to Esau.

debates: What the two camps of Mahanaim are: the angels and Jacob's own company, two companies of angels flanking him, the angels of Mesopotamia handing him to those of Canaan, or a dual standing simply for a plural
Whether each believer has one guardian angel, which Henry declines to dispute and Calvin calls a depreciation of God's kindness
outliers: Clarke suspends the exposition twice, once for a lexical and patristic note on the word angel closing with a passage of Hesiod on guardian spirits, and once for a polemic against the invocation of angels
Ellicott records that numberless conjectures have been hazarded to explain the angels away as prophets, traders or a rescue party sent by Rebekah

3.pericope_label: The embassy to Esau, the report of four hundred men, and the divided company

schools.summary: Gill identifies the messengers as Jacob's own servants against Jarchi's reading of angels, and judges the alarm a plain failure of faith after so many promises and the appearance of the angelic guard; Calvin states and answers the objection that Jacob cedes the dominion he had fought for, denies that the wealth is named in boasting, reads Esau's removal to Seir as providence leaving the land vacant, cites Malachi to make the voluntary departure a banishment, conjectures that Rebekah sent the news, explains why God let a groundless fear stand, warns that faith is never exempt from fear, and notes that the word for the two bands is the word behind Mahanaim.

Henry explains why Jacob would not pass by an offended elder brother without civility, reads the titles as a disclaimer of the birthright's prerogatives, defends the fear as consistent with humble confidence since Christ in his agony was sorely amazed, observes that the troubles of the righteous succeed one another as clouds return after rain, and marks that the company was divided for flight and not, as Abraham's was, for fight.

Clarke notes that messengers and angels are the same word, dates the embassy before the Mahanaim vision, places Seir from the Dead Sea to the Arabian gulf and finds Esau's sword-prophecy fulfilled in his dispossessing the Horites, denies that the four hundred men were hostile at all, lays Jacob's terror to a guilty conscience with a tag from Horace on the brazen wall, and calls the dividing of the flocks prudence turned into a right channel; Wesley follows Henry on the titles and adds that Jacob came neither as fugitive nor beggar.

Ellicott reconstructs Esau's Horite raid from Hebron and explains how it led him afterwards to settle in Seir, notes that Seir means rough and the term field marks an uncultivated region, measures the hundred miles from Mahanaim and traces Esau's approach through the later Moab and Ammon, reads the catalogue of wealth as a disclaimer of any claim on Isaac's property, and calls Jacob's faith feeble but real because it drove him to prayer; Keil and Delitzsch pass from the two bands directly to the prayer.

debates: Whether Esau's four hundred men were a hostile force, which Gill and Henry assume, or an honourable escort, as Clarke and Calvin both conclude
Whether Jacob's terror was a failure of faith, as Gill and Ellicott judge, or consistent with faith, as Henry argues and Calvin explains
outliers: Calvin raises against himself the objection that Jacob's submission surrenders everything he had risked his life to obtain, and answers by distinguishing the temporal dominion from the secret benediction

schools.summary: Gill prefers the marginal rendering that Jacob is less than all the mercies, and takes the confession to disclaim any merit for temporal or spiritual favours alike; Calvin finds in the prayer the proof that fear had not overcome faith, explains the covenant titles as God's condescension and as a mark distinguishing him from idols, makes the command and the promise the two pillars of the petition, calls it holy boldness to ask for what God has bound himself to give, argues that Jacob's appeal proves he had not lied to his wives about the command to return, sets the plea of unworthiness against Satan's discouragement, and reads the mother with the children as a proverb drawn from hawking.

Henry makes times of fear times of prayer and notes that Jacob applied to God rather than to the angels he had just seen or to Laban's teraphim, explains why he called God the God of his fathers rather than his own, calls the plea of unworthiness surprising and compares those whom Christ commended, quotes Herbert's motto, turns the two bands into a measure of increase, and lays down that the best we can say to God is what he has said to us.

Clarke sets out the prayer as a model in five constituents, prefers the marginal rendering and compares Paul's less than the least of all saints, follows the Chaldee in taking the staff to mean Jacob alone without attendants, infers from the mother with the children how fiercely Jacob feared his brother, and observes that he stopped when he reached the promise that ratified the covenant; Wesley follows Henry closely on the covenant titles, the plea of unworthiness and the staff.

Ellicott calls this the first recorded prayer in Scripture and traces its movement from the God of the fathers to the Jehovah who commanded the return, dwells on the picture of the mother slain upon her children as Hosea's image of the worst of war's miseries, and observes that with God, unlike with men, pleading a former favour is not ungenerous since each act of mercy pledges more; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the same phrase as proverbial for unsparing cruelty, drawn from the bird covering its young.

debates: Why God is addressed as the God of Abraham and Isaac: Henry and Wesley read it as self-denial declining to claim him as Jacob's own, Calvin as God's own condescension and as the mark distinguishing him from the idols
outliers: Clarke and Gill both set aside the Authorised Version's I am not worthy for the marginal I am less than all the mercies, and Calvin renders it the same way from the Latin

13.pericope_label: The present sent before him, and the crossing of the Jabbok

schools.summary: Gill explains why the drovers are made to repeat that Jacob follows, since the present would have counted for nothing without the visit and Esau would have thought himself slighted; Calvin warns against contriving subterfuges after prayer while insisting that security must not breed indolence, contrasts the diligence of the pious with the world's restless activity, measures the size of the gift against the value Jacob set on the promise and rebukes those who will not bear to be losers, explains the proleptic naming of the Jabbok, holds that Jacob stayed behind for solitude in prayer, and draws a threefold order of prayer, means and courage.

Henry makes the present the complement of the prayer, observing that fear did not dispirit Jacob from using means nor prayer make him presume without them, counts the beasts at five hundred and eighty, finds in them proof of God's blessing and of Jacob's wisdom in parting with some to secure the rest, thinks tame cattle a shrewd gift for a hunter newly settled, and holds that a friendly confidence in men's goodness may prevent the mischief their badness designs.

Clarke calls the present princely and sufficient to compensate the loss of birthright and blessing, dwells on the value of milch camels among the Arabs with a citation from Pliny on their milk, prefers the received ten bulls to the twenty of the Syriac and Vulgate, treats the whole transaction as restitution for an injury, glosses what came to his hand as what providence had put in his power, and places the Jabbok's rise in Gilead; Wesley follows Henry on the humble message and the confidence it expressed.

Ellicott judges that faith had regained the ascendancy since Jacob put everything into Esau's power, renders the space between the droves a breathing place, takes I will appease him literally as covering the face with the offering and connects it with the legal term for atonement, reports and rejects the Jewish reading of precious stones, identifies the Jabbok as the Wady Zerka with Tristram's account of the ford, and argues from the width of the ravine and from Peniel's lying in Gad that Jacob remained on its southern side; Keil and Delitzsch make the herd five hundred and fifty, match the selection to nomad holdings as in Job, and find the proportion of males to females following Varro's rule.

debates: The size of the present: Henry counts five hundred and eighty head where Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both count five hundred and fifty
Where Jacob was left alone: Ellicott argues from the ravine's width and from Peniel's lying in Gad that he stayed on the south side, against the common assumption that he recrossed the stream
outliers: Clarke reads the whole present as restitution and adds that one who can make restitution for a wrong and will not has no claim even on the mercy of God

24.pericope_label: The wrestling at the Jabbok and the dislocated thigh

schools.summary: Gill calls the wrestler the Son of God in the form of man and explains that he prevailed not because he would not, Jacob's pleading of the promises leaving him no other course; Calvin insists that God himself and not Satan or a mortal was the antagonist, takes the vision as a picture of every believer's conflict, answers the objection that no one can contend with God by showing that he furnishes the weapons and defends with one hand while assailing with the other, explains why the trial came only now and why it came at the border of the promised land, notes that Moses speaks after the manner of men in making the angel retire, and makes the lasting wound the proof that victory comes only through injury.

Henry leaves the wrestler's identity open between a created angel and the eternal Word, describes the combat as hand to hand with God seeming to dispute the pass, draws from Hosea that the weapons were prayers and tears, explains that the angel's not prevailing means Jacob's faith was not shaken, thinks the pain was not felt since he did not halt till the struggle ended, and reads the request to be released as a condescension meant to honour a faith that would rather be dislocated than unblessed.

Clarke identifies the wrestler outright as the Lord Jesus Christ and argues at length that the body was appearance only, since bodies really assumed could not vanish instantly, doubts that the thigh was fully dislocated and suggests a disabling blow healed by sunrise, and denies that daybreak had anything to do with apparitions fleeing the light, most angelic appearances in Scripture having occurred in open day; Wesley follows Henry closely on the angel's not prevailing, the strength derived from heaven, and the painless wound.

Ellicott derives the rare verb from a word for dust and connects it with the name Jabbok, denies that the angel was an incarnation of Deity and calls the event a mediate manifestation prefiguring the incarnation, rejects the allegorical reading as contradicted by the new name and the lameness, takes the hollow for the hip socket and the injury for a sprain, renders the parting words as send me away and treats the request as an admission of defeat, and reports the Jewish notion that the wrestler was Esau's protecting angel; Keil and Delitzsch place Jacob on the northern side of the Jabbok and derive the verb from a root meaning to plant limb against limb.

debates: Who the wrestler was: Clarke says plainly the Lord Jesus Christ, Gill the Son of God in human form, Calvin God himself, Ellicott a mediate manifestation through a messenger and expressly not an incarnation, while Henry declines to decide
Whether the body was real or only apparent, Clarke arguing at length that angels never assume substance
Which side of the Jabbok Jacob was left on, Keil and Delitzsch saying the northern and Ellicott arguing for the southern
What the injury was: a dislocation, a disabling blow to the groin healed by morning, or a sprain of the hip socket
outliers: Ellicott records a Jewish tradition that the wrestler was the angel charged with defending Esau, overpowered by Jacob with the aid of his own guardian

27.pericope_label: The new name, Peniel, and the shrunken sinew

schools.summary: Gill explains why Jacob was emboldened to ask the wrestler's name and what kind of name he hoped for, identifies Penuel and its later city, reads the rising sun as an emblem of the Sun of righteousness, and calls the abstinence from the sinew very superstitious, citing the Mishnah's rules; Calvin follows Jerome on the sense of the new name, insists that the old name is not abolished and that God gives with a name the thing it implies, explains the refusal of the divine name by the twilight in which the fathers walked, commends the monument at Peniel as public rather than private, argues that God's glory would destroy us unsustained, thinks the halting painless so that the miracle might be plainer, and expressly denies that the abstinence was superstition.

Clarke offers two derivations of Israel and connects the second with the name Peniel, prefers a literal rendering of the clause about prevailing with God and men, suspects that Jacob sought a name by which to invoke the angel and that this might have bred idolatry, notes a Septuagint addition apparently borrowed from the story of Manoah, asks whether Malachi's Sun of righteousness looks back to this sunrise and suggests the thigh was healed with the dawn, and refuses to conjecture which sinew is meant; Wesley reports the exchange of names and the honour of being a prince with God, and holds that if Jacob limped to his grave the honour countervailed the damage.

Ellicott renders Israel a prince of God and matches the new name to a changed character, gives an alternative sense for the last clause, compares the refusal of a name to Manoah's case, would read Penuel here as in the next verse, argues that Jacob discovered his lameness only when he tried to walk and his sinews cooled, and identifies the sinew as the great tendon from the spinal cord while reporting the Jewish view that this was the second ordinance laid on Abraham's race; Keil and Delitzsch derive Israel from a verb meaning to fight, name the nerve nearest the hip as the one most easily injured in wrestling, and observe that the custom holds still.

debates: Whether the sunrise marks a healing, as Clarke suggests from Malachi, or the moment when the cooling sinews first revealed the injury, as Ellicott argues
Whether the abstinence from the sinew is superstition, as Gill judges, or the lawful discipline of the Church in its infancy, as Calvin insists
Why Jacob asked the wrestler's name: to remember the occasion, as Gill supposes, to invoke him afterwards, as Clarke suspects, or from a pious desire for fuller knowledge of God, as Calvin argues
outliers: Calvin reports that the Jews of his own time could no longer identify the forbidden sinew or even which thigh it lay in, and therefore abstained from both hind quarters and sold those parts to Christians
Clarke records that the Aldine Septuagint and several manuscripts add the words which is wonderful to the angel's refusal, apparently borrowed from the parallel in Judges

Henry has no block keyed within these verses; his exposition of the naming, the refused name and the blessing stands at verse twenty-four and is used in the entry there. Wesley's notes here reproduce that exposition almost word for word, so the puritan-evangelical substance survives without the voice.
